questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step that narrows an over-broad design question
questions.stem: A design brief asks the team to improve the entire cooling arrangement for a server rack. What is the best first narrowing step?

options.text: Restate the broad request as one measurable question about airflow at the rack inlet.
Survey every cooling subsystem at once so the team cannot miss an important option.
options.misconception: believes wide coverage counts as a narrowed question

options.text: Keep the request worded broadly until the team has listed every cooling idea worth trying.
options.misconception: assumes narrowing always throws away useful options

options.text: Pick the rack with the highest recorded inlet temperature and use it as the case study.
options.misconception: confuses choosing a test case with narrowing the question

questions.explanation: Narrowing turns a broad goal into one answerable question, and inlet airflow is measurable. Surveying every subsystem keeps the scope wide, while picking one rack swaps a topic for a single case.
questions.hint: Ask which single question the brief must answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Identify the evidence that would settle a question
questions.stem: A brief asks whether a proposed pump cuts peak electricity use by eight percent. What must be established before the question can be answered?

answer.exemplar: The claim is only answerable once the baseline and the measurement window are fixed. The team must record the present peak draw over a defined operating period, specify whether eight percent is measured against that peak or against average consumption, and name the instrument and tolerance that will be used. Without those three items the comparison can be run in ways that produce whatever number the writer wanted.

questions.explanation: Answerability turns on whether the evidence can settle the question. Here the baseline, the metric and the measurement window are missing, so almost any figure could be produced.
questions.hint: Ask what data already exists and what it can support.

questions.learningObjective: Detect a question that smuggles in its answer

questions.explanation: The third question treats the increase as settled and asks only for objections, so it can only draw a defence. The other phrasings leave the outcome open.

questions.topic: Assumptions carried by a borrowed method

questions.stem: The team adopts a standard reliability method from a mature field to check a new mechanism. What must the team examine first?

options.misconception: confuses document style with method validity

options.text: How quickly the standard can be learned by engineers new to the method.
options.misconception: assumes training difficulty predicts technical error

options.misconception: treats prior use as proof of transferability

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limit of an analogy
questions.stem: A brief compares a cooling loop to a garden hose. Explain the point at which this comparison stops being useful.

answer.exemplar: The hose analogy helps with the idea that flow depends on pressure difference and on restrictions along the path, so it illuminates why a blocked filter lowers flow. It stops carrying once the team reasons about heat capacity, boiling, phase change or the control loop, because a hose carries fluid at ambient temperature and none of those phenomena have a counterpart in the analogy. The moment a decision depends on a property the hose lacks, the comparison must be set aside.

questions.explanation: An analogy is useful only for the structure it shares, and a hose shares flow and restriction but not heat transfer. Once the argument turns on properties the hose lacks, it misleads.
questions.hint: Ask which property the decision actually depends on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Recognise vocabulary with no local counterpart
questions.stem: Explain what a reader should do when the brief uses a word from another field that has no counterpart in this one.

answer.exemplar: The reader should stop treating the imported word as if it carried a settled meaning and instead work out what the writer intends in this discipline. That means finding the sentence where the term does the real work, listing the properties being attributed to it, and writing those properties out in the vocabulary of the field at hand. If no local term covers them, the writer should coin a plain description and keep using it consistently rather than borrowing a word that suggests the wrong properties.

questions.explanation: A word with no counterpart cannot be translated by finding a synonym, so the reader must unpack what it means and re-express it locally. A near-match imports properties this field lacks.
questions.hint: Unpack the borrowed word into local properties.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the embedded conclusion in a wording
questions.stem: Explain how a reviewer can tell that a question in the brief has already assumed its own answer.

answer.exemplar: The reviewer should read the question as if it were a proposed conclusion rather than a request, and check whether a yes answer adds nothing while a no answer sounds like an error or an obstruction. Phrases such as surely, clearly and any reason to doubt do the work. A second test is to rewrite the question in the opposite direction and see whether the rewritten version could plausibly be the one the writer actually meant to ask; if it could, the original was steering the answer.

questions.explanation: A leading question smuggles in the answer through its wording, so the test is to ask what a no answer would mean and whether it is treated as unthinkable. Reversing the direction shows the steering.
questions.hint: Try reversing the direction of the expected answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Apply narrowing to a design request
questions.stem: Describe how you would narrow the topic of a brief that asks for a more reliable product.

answer.exemplar: I would first split the vague quality word into the ways reliability can fail, such as hardware failure, manufacturing variation, operator error and supply of spares. Then I would pick the failure mode that the brief has the authority and the data to attack, and restate the request as a question about that mode alone. The result is narrow because one failure mode can be measured and a fix can be judged against it, unlike the original phrase which could support any project at all.

questions.explanation: Narrowing works by splitting a vague quality into distinguishable failure modes and committing to one that can be measured. Without that step, any project can claim to improve reliability.
questions.hint: Split the vague word into ways it can fail.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Assumptions carried by a borrowed method
questions.learningObjective: Surface the assumptions a borrowed method imports
questions.stem: Explain what a borrowed method carries with it that most teams forget to check.

answer.exemplar: A borrowed method carries a set of premises about the situation it was designed for: what counts as a normal case, what causes failure, how stable the inputs are, and what level of measurement the method expects. Transferring the method without those premises means applying its conclusions to a case it was never fitted to, and the resulting numbers look precise while describing the wrong situation. The habit worth building is to write down the method's premises and mark which ones hold here.

questions.explanation: Methods carry assumptions about normal cases, failure causes and measurement quality. A team that checks results but not premises ends up applying conclusions fitted to a different situation.
questions.hint: Write down what the method takes for granted.

answer.exemplar: The team should ask what evidence exists today, what would have to be measured, and whether the measurement would actually separate the possible answers. questions.explanation: The rewrite that works names the measure of noise, the use the product is put to and the threshold for worth, so a result could settle the matter. The alternatives keep the assumption.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Apply a definition-first rule to a brief
questions.stem: Which sequence fixes an ambiguous term that carries a recommendation in the brief?

options.text: State what the term denotes in this brief, then check that the recommendation follows from that sense.
Ask the reviewer which sense was meant, then rewrite the recommendation to match it.
options.misconception: lets a later reader settle the meaning

options.text: Rewrite the recommendation to avoid the term, then leave the term as it stands.
options.misconception: removes the symptom and keeps the ambiguity

options.text: Move the term to the glossary, then keep using it in the body of the brief.
options.misconception: hides the term while leaving its uses untouched

questions.explanation: The sense has to be settled first, and only then can a reader check whether the recommendation follows from it. Deferring the decision or avoiding the word leaves the reader guessing.
questions.hint: Settle the sense, then test the recommendation.
